831.event_title: Decca Records turns down the Beatles
831.event: Through their manager Brian Epstein, the Beatles were given an audition at Decca Records' studios in north London on New Year's Day 1962, recording about fifteen songs. Decca turned them down and instead signed Brian Poole and the Tremeloes, another group that auditioned that day. Later in 1962 the Beatles were signed by EMI's Parlophone label under producer George Martin and went on to become the most successful band in popular music.
831.explanation: The decision became one of the best-known missed opportunities in business history, though Decca's executives acted on their judgement of a young, unproven group.
831.tie_back: The kural defines folly as taking hold of what brings loss and letting slip what would bring profit, and Decca chose the lesser act and let the Beatles go to a rival.
831._accuracy_note: Illustrates letting a great gain slip away, but the choice was an honest error of judgement rather than a fool's grasp at harm, and the famous remark attributed to Decca's Dick Rowe is disputed and omitted here.

832.event_title: Muhammad ibn Tughluq moves his capital to Daulatabad
832.event: Sultan Muhammad ibn Tughluq of Delhi moved his capital to Deogiri in the western Deccan, renamed Daulatabad, in order to strengthen his hold on the south, and large numbers of people from Delhi were moved there. Soon after he was established in the Deccan, rebellions broke out in the north, on the western frontier and in Bengal, and he had to return to Delhi. His transfer of the capital and his introduction of a token currency are both counted among his ambitious schemes that failed and caused great hardship.
832.explanation: The sultan's projects were bold, but they were poorly executed and beyond what his government could carry out, and they stirred opposition across his realm.
832.tie_back: The kural calls it the worst folly to set one's heart on deeds that are not fitting for oneself, read by some commentators as deeds beyond one's ability, and the forced move of the capital was such an undertaking.
832._accuracy_note: Fits the reading of deeds beyond one's capacity, but the traditional reading of the kural concerns deeds unsuited to one's moral conduct, which the event does not show.

833.event_title: The six-month reign of Tsar Peter III
833.event: Peter III became emperor of Russia in January 1762, while Russia was fighting Prussia in the Seven Years' War, and in May he made peace with Frederick II of Prussia and withdrew Russia from the war, giving up its gains. He planned a war against Denmark on behalf of his German duchy of Holstein, offended the Orthodox Church by pressing changes in its practices, and alienated the imperial guards by threatening to disband them. In July 1762, about six months after his accession, his wife Catherine and the guards overthrew him, and she took the throne as Catherine II.
833.explanation: Peter III showed little regard for his subjects' feelings or his country's interests, and in a few months he lost the support of every group that mattered.
833.tie_back: The kural lists the fool's habits as shamelessness, not seeking what is worth seeking, lack of affection and caring for nothing, and Peter III's brief reign showed indifference to the Russia he had been given to rule.
833._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial fit: Peter's disregard for Russian interests is documented, but the kural's fourfold catalogue of personal vices is broader than what the sources record.

834.event_title: Charles Van Doren admits the quiz show Twenty-One was rigged
834.event: Charles Van Doren, an English instructor at Columbia University from a celebrated literary family, became a national celebrity by winning $129,000 on the NBC quiz show Twenty-One in 1956-57. After denying the rigging to the press, the public and a grand jury, he testified before a congressional committee in November 1959 that he had been given the answers in advance and coached on how to perform. Columbia accepted his resignation, NBC ended his contract, and he later pleaded guilty to perjury and received a suspended sentence.
834.explanation: A scholar who taught literature and was celebrated as a model of learning had taken part in a deception watched by millions.
834.tie_back: The kural says no fool is greater than one who has studied, understood and taught others yet does not live by what he learned, and Van Doren, a university teacher, lived for years in a public lie.
834._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a learned teacher failing to live by his learning, though the kural speaks of moral teachings and Van Doren's subject was literature.

835.event_title: Thomas Austin releases rabbits at Barwon Park
835.place: Barwon Park, near Geelong, Victoria, Australia
835.event: Shortly after Christmas 1859, twenty-four European wild rabbits imported from England by the grazier Thomas Austin arrived in Melbourne, and Austin released some of them on his Barwon Park property so that he and his friends could hunt them. The rabbits multiplied rapidly, crossing into New South Wales by 1880, reaching Queensland in 1886 and Western Australia in 1894. Genetic research has traced most of Australia's rabbits to this release, and they became one of the country's most destructive pests, damaging crops, pasture and native plants for generations.
835.explanation: A single act done for one man's sport created a problem that has cost Australia's land and farmers dearly for more than a century and a half.
835.tie_back: The kural says the fool can in one lifetime create a hell that lasts through seven births, and Austin's release of a few rabbits caused harm that has lasted through many generations.
835._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of one act's damage lasting for generations, reading the kural in Kalaignar's this-worldly sense; Austin did not foresee the consequences, and the traditional reading concerns punishment across rebirths.

836.event_title: Francis I is defeated and captured at Pavia
836.event: During his war with Emperor Charles V, King Francis I of France laid siege to Pavia, and in the battle against the imperial relief army he led his armoured cavalry in a charge with couched lances. The charge put his horsemen where his own artillery could no longer fire on the enemy, and Spanish arquebusiers inflicted heavy losses on the French. Francis was captured, taken to Spain and held in Madrid for more than a year, and was released only after signing the Treaty of Madrid in January 1526.
836.explanation: The king's old-fashioned tactics against an army using firearms not only lost the battle but made him a prisoner of his rival.
836.tie_back: The kural says that when one who does not know how to do a thing takes it on, the work fails and he ends up putting himself in chains, and Francis's ill-judged charge lost the battle and his own freedom.
836._accuracy_note: A close fit for the double penalty of failed work and the doer's own captivity, though Francis was an experienced commander misled by outdated tactics rather than a complete novice.

837.event_title: Khedive Ismail's debts bring Egypt under European financial control
837.event: Khedive Ismail of Egypt financed costly modernisation projects and other ambitions largely with loans from European financiers, and the national debt rose many times over during his reign. In 1875 he sold Egypt's Suez Canal shares to Britain, and in 1876, unable to meet payments, Egypt's finances were placed under the supervision of a European debt commission and British and French controllers. In June 1879 the Ottoman sultan, pressed by Britain and France, deposed Ismail in favour of his son Tawfiq.
837.explanation: Ismail's borrowing enriched foreign bondholders while the burden of repayment fell on Egypt, and it ended in the loss of control over the country's own finances.
837.tie_back: The kural says that when a fool comes into great wealth, strangers feast while his own people go hungry, and Egypt's wealth under Ismail flowed to foreign creditors while Egyptians bore the cost.
837._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial fit: Ismail's spending had real modernising aims and he was not simply a fool, and the sources do not document Egyptians going hungry as a direct result.

838.event_title: Ceausescu builds the House of the People
838.event: From 1984 the Romanian leader Nicolae Ceausescu had an enormous government palace, the House of the People, built in Bucharest, and the project required clearing large areas of the historic city centre. Thousands of workers and hundreds of architects worked on it during the 1980s, a time when Romania was struggling to feed its own people and the costs were enormous. The building was still unfinished when Ceausescu fell in December 1989, and it now houses Romania's Parliament.
838.explanation: Absolute power let one man pour a struggling nation's resources into a monument to himself.
838.tie_back: The kural compares a fool who comes into possession of something to a madman who is also drunk, and unchecked control of a country led Ceausescu into one of the most extravagant building projects of the century.
838._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of possession magnifying folly, though Ceausescu's rule involved far more than folly and the kural's image of intoxication is figurative.

839.event_title: General Charles Lee is suspended and then dismissed from the Continental Army
839.place: Monmouth, New Jersey, and Philadelphia, United States
839.event: Major General Charles Lee, second in rank in the Continental Army, led the advance at the Battle of Monmouth in June 1778, but his attack faltered and his troops fell back in disorder until George Washington rallied them. At his own request Lee was court-martialed and was found guilty of disobeying orders, misbehaviour before the enemy and disrespect to Washington, and was suspended for a year. He continued to attack his accusers and Congress, was dismissed from the army in January 1780, and the army carried on under Washington without him.
839.explanation: Lee's departure removed a quarrelsome and unreliable senior officer, and it cost the American cause nothing.
839.tie_back: The kural says ironically that friendship with fools is sweet because nothing is lost when it ends, and the army's parting with Lee caused no loss at all.
839._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Lee was an experienced but erratic officer rather than a fool and a colleague rather than a friend of Washington, so only the painless parting matches the kural.

840.event_title: George Psalmanazar's false Formosa deceives learned London
840.event: A young Frenchman who called himself George Psalmanazar arrived in London around 1703 claiming to be a native of Formosa (Taiwan), and in 1704 published a description of the island, which he had never visited, complete with an invented alphabet and language. He was received in learned circles, including the Royal Society and the Bishop of London, until other experts showed his claims to be false and he became a target of satire. In his memoirs, published in 1764 after his death, he admitted the imposture.
840.explanation: An impostor with no real knowledge entered the gatherings of scholars and, once exposed, became a byword for fraud.
840.tie_back: The kural likens a fool entering an assembly of the wise to setting unwashed feet on a clean bed, and Psalmanazar's appearance among London's learned societies brought falsehood into a place meant for knowledge.
840._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for an unfit person in an assembly of the learned, though Psalmanazar was a clever impostor rather than a fool, and the scholars were initially deceived by him.
